title: The Nasdaq Just Had Its Worst Day in a Year. Indian American Tech Workers Felt Every Point.
excerpt: Chip stocks collapsed, rate-hike odds surged past 70 per cent, and the nine-week rally ended in a single session. For a community whose paychecks, RSUs, and retirement savings are concentrated in the sector that fell hardest, this is personal.
body:
The Nasdaq Composite plunged 4.2 per cent on Friday — its steepest single-day fall in over a year — as a hotter-than-expected jobs report collided with fading confidence in the AI trade. For Indian American tech professionals, whose financial lives are uniquely tied to the sector, the selloff is not just a market event. It is a personal one.

## What Happened

The trigger was the May jobs report: 172,000 new positions, more than double the 80,000 economists had forecast. The unemployment rate held at 4.3 per cent, and average hourly earnings rose 3.6 per cent year-over-year. On its own, the labour market strength would be welcome news. But it landed on a market already rattled by Broadcom's weaker-than-expected AI chip guidance earlier in the week.

The combination sent Treasury yields surging. The 10-year yield jumped to 4.53 per cent. Traders now see a roughly 70 per cent chance that the Federal Reserve will raise rates by year-end — up from less than 50 per cent before the report. The two-year yield climbed to 4.16 per cent, its highest level in a year.

The damage was concentrated in the stocks that had led the market higher for nine consecutive weeks. Nvidia fell 6.2 per cent. Broadcom dropped 7.9 per cent. Marvell Technology collapsed 16.7 per cent. Micron, AMD, Intel, Qualcomm, and ARM all shed more than 10 per cent. The semiconductor index (.SOX) recorded its worst day of 2026.

The S&P 500 fell 2.6 per cent, ending nine straight weeks of Friday-to-Friday gains — its longest such streak since December 2023. The Dow held up better, down 1.4 per cent.

## Why This Hits Indian Americans Harder

Indian Americans are disproportionately exposed to this selloff in ways that most demographic groups are not. The community is heavily concentrated in technology — roughly 70 per cent of H-1B visa holders work in tech and related fields, and Indian-born professionals represent a significant share of engineering and management roles at the very companies that fell hardest: Nvidia, Google, Microsoft, Meta, and the broader semiconductor supply chain.

That exposure goes beyond paychecks. Restricted stock units (RSUs), which vest over multi-year schedules, are a central pillar of tech compensation. When Nvidia drops 6 per cent in a single session, it is not just portfolio pain — it is a direct reduction in expected income for thousands of Indian American engineers holding unvested RSUs. The same applies to stock options, which lose intrinsic value rapidly in sharp selloffs.

Then there is the 401(k) concentration. Many tech workers default into growth-heavy allocations — QQQ-tracking funds, S&P 500 growth indices, or company stock. A 5 per cent weekly decline in the Nasdaq erases weeks of compounding.

## The Rate-Hike Risk for NRIs

For non-resident Indians managing money across two economies, the rate picture is particularly complicated. If the Fed hikes, the dollar strengthens further against the rupee — which has already been Asia's worst-performing currency this year. That makes remittances cheaper in dollar terms but erodes the purchasing power of rupee-denominated assets.

Meanwhile, the RBI just doubled NRI equity investment limits in Indian stocks, from 5 per cent to 10 per cent per company. The timing creates an interesting asymmetry: as US tech valuations compress, Indian equities — trading at more moderate multiples — may start looking more attractive to NRI capital. The Sensex fell 244 points on Friday after the RBI held rates, but at 74,143 it remains well below the stretched valuations of US tech.

## What to Do Now

"After the record run we've seen the last nine weeks in equities, specifically tech and semiconductors, the dam just broke today," said Ryan Detrick, chief market strategist at Carson Group. "Obviously, the stronger-than-expected jobs report puts the Fed in a tough spot."

But most strategists are not calling this the end of the bull market. "The market reaction today was more driven by positioning rather than fundamentals," said Ohsung Kwon, chief equity strategist at Wells Fargo. "The semiconductor sector was way overbought."

For Indian American tech workers, the playbook is straightforward: review RSU concentration (the standard advice is never to hold more than 10-15 per cent of net worth in a single stock), rebalance 401(k) allocations toward diversified holdings, and consider whether the new RBI rules make Indian equities worth a closer look. The nine-week party is over. The question is whether this is a hangover or a turning point.

*Sources: Reuters, Wall Street Journal, Barron's, Investor's Business Daily, CME Group*
